chapter: Minton's, Louis Armstrong and the South
title: "Take your hat off": drugstore insult, and the army stable horses
summary: The druggist told George Washington to take his hat off with a slur; Clarke then recalls riding horses at a segregated army-area stable, owned by a Black groom who charged $2.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: a hat. I've always liked them. And so I had this tam on, and George was standing at the door with his hat on. And after I said, "Well, how much will that be?" "Well, just a minute, we'll figure it out." So he figured it out and said, that will be so and so. I said okay. So I paid him and he said, "Goodbye, sir," and he looked over at George and said, "Nigger, take your hat off!" Can you imagine that? It's been like that all the time. I can remember my experiences in the South, when I was in the army. I love horses. So I saw -- this is a similar experience. I saw beautiful horses, you know, and these white guys were riding these horses. I thought, damn, I've got to ride a horse. That's my sport. I love it, you know? So I asked one of the sergeants, I said, "Where is a stable?" He said, "Man, there's an old cracker down there, and I wouldn't go down there if I were you." I said, "Well, shit, I'm going to ride a horse. All he can do is say, 'Get out of here'." So there was a guy from Texas, really good, he was really a horseman from his heart, and a trumpet player, too. He wanted to ride, but no-one wanted to ask the guy. So I said, "Show me where the stables are." Now, this is the God's truth, and I walked in, and a guy said right there, right there, just turn in. So I turned into the stable and I saw this horse, and there was a colored kid grooming him, you know. So I walked in and said, "I'd sure like to ride one of those fine horses you have here." I said, "I've seen a couple down the street." He

said, "Oh, yeah, they're pretty good horses. You pick yourself out one." You know. So he said, "Come here a minute. I want to ask you a question." And I had my uniform on. He said, "Now, I wouldn't ask a white man this because he'd think I was dumb, but who are we fighting this time?" He said, "It's them damned Germans, ain't it?" I said, "You guessed it." He said, "I knew it." So he said, "Which horse do you want?" I said, "Wait a minute. I'll take that one, but I have a couple of friends of mine I would like." He said, "Bring them in." Now, there's no colored man had ever rode his horses before. I didn't find it out till after. And we took those horses all over the place. You know, in the woods, woods, woods, and we just rode till we got tired. And I come back, and when I came back he said, "Did you have a good time?" I said, "Yeah, how much do I owe you?"
That side quit just before you said to the guy, "How much do I owe you?"
Yeah. I asked him how much I owed him. He said, "Give me $2.00." So I thought that was really fantastic.
Because he appreciated the fact that I had informed him about who we were at war with, and that he was afraid to ask a white man, because he said, "They'll think
I'm dumb." Yeah. That's a wonderful story. Now, we've got to go back to where we were.
